newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Switzerland's Oerlikon, Bally rift widens.
newsitem.headline: Switzerland's Oerlikon, Bally rift widens.

text.p: The only thing going public now are grievances at Swiss conglomerate Oerlikon-Buerhle Holding AG after its chairman ruled out a bourse listing for its shoe unit Bally last week.

The squabble has become more heated ahead of August 18, when Bally chief executive Ernst Thomke is expected to make an internal presentation at an annual Oerlikon strategy session on his plans to revamp Bally.

Thomke, a turn-around specialist credited with success at other companies including watchmaker SMH, said in an interview with a Swiss newspaper on Sunday he would not rule out leaving Bally, where he was appointed CEO in September 1995.
"It (resignation) is a possibility, because there are certain things I cannot accept," Thomke said in the interview in the SonntagsZeitung on Sunday.
Such a public dispute is a rarity at one of Switzerland's old family firms, in which the Swiss Buerhle family still holds roughly 30 percent.

"It is certainly very unusual," said Edwin van der Geest, corporate spokesman for Saurer AG, who also speaks for Thomke, commenting on the dispute. Saurer is another company where Thomke has been instrumental in restructuring.

Van der Geest confirmed that Thomke was correctly quoted in the SonntagsZeitung interview. In the interview Thomke criticised a press statement sent out earlier last week by his boss Hans Widmer, chairman of Oerlikon.

Thomke said in Sunday's interview that his disappointment stemmed in part from the fact that he had reached an agreement with Widmer not to make any more public statements about Bally until after the August 18 meeting.
Widmer said Wednesday that Oerlikon's board of directors "believe the concrete conditions are not appropriate for going public (with Bally)."
Thomke has also dismissed any notion that he was keen for a public listing of Bally, hoping to personally gain from this.

One source close to Thomke said the Bally CEO was also insulted by an interview published in June in the Swiss magazine Cash, in which Hortense Anda-Buerhle, the dominant Buehrle family shareholder and a member of Oerlikon's board, criticised Thomke.
Anda-Buehrle was quoted by Cash as saying of Thomke: "He should quit talking. What is needed now is hard work."

Ironically, some analysts believed that Widmer's latest statement on Wednesday, following a series of press articles about the dispute, was designed to pacify Thomke, signalling that Oerlikon was willing to put money into Bally.
Widmer said in a separate article printed a week ago in the tabloid "Blick",that it was in "national interest" that Thomke remain at the helm of Bally.
Widmer said last Wednesday that Thomke, at a meeting on May 21, told Oerlikon's board the restructuring of Bally was going more slowly and taking more time than expected.
Thomke confirmed in Sunday's interview he had under-estimated the cost of restructuring Bally, put initially at 100 million Swiss francs. Swiss press estimates put the amount needed at 150 million.

Julius Baer equities analyst Beat Kunz said it would be positive for Oerlikon and Bally if Thomke stayed. Bally has had a long series of management changes and is only now starting to show signs of profitability, he said.

Oerlikon's share price lost 10 percent in the last two weeks as a result of the dispute, Kunz said. On Monday afternoon, Oerlikon was quoted down 3.25 Swiss francs at 150.75, although the Swiss stock market was weaker Monday, too.
Oerlikon also owns weapons and aerospace Contraves Group, semiconductor and vacuum technology firm Balzers & Leybold, and airplane maker Pilatus. The firm declined to comment.
